claims_disputed.claim: Cumulative cost never exceeds (1+eps) times agent-only cost.
claims_disputed.reason: Theorem 4.1 is a by-construction budget invariant, and its proof is sound. But it holds only against a modeled reference: §2 defines A_t as 'a model-based comparison, not an extra agent execution observed on each task', and it requires known finite charge bounds that 'historical means alone do not ensure' (§4.3, §7). In the live study (App. D.2), one task was denied service, which 'falls outside the theorem's assumption'. The 4800 + 120 runs that stay within 1.25 are simulations using the same fixed charges, so they check the implementation, not real spend.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The per-use win (saving shares 0.936–0.999; 178/180 vs 157/180 successes, App. A.4 Table 6) is measured only on programs that already passed verification. That is survivorship: 9 of 20 compilation cells failed (§3.2), and the matched replays used a different emulator profile (A.8). End to end, compiling without PACE's savings test costs about 1.53× PACE on the logs (Table 4, +52.68%), i.e. more than never compiling (ReAct ≈ 1.26× PACE, Table 3). PACE itself is costlier than ReAct on Sepsis for all three models. Compile-to-code therefore pays off only under a careful decision rule, which is consistent with the review's own P28 'mixed' for the same mechanism. The mapping to CodeAct/code-as-action is also loose.

missed_issues: Silent failures: App. A.7 reports that only about 58%, 87% and 71% of program test failures (GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen) raise a detectable execution error. The rest leave an incorrect task state with no error. This violates the cost model's detected-failure assumption (§2), which the paper admits; under it, fallback never triggers for those runs. For an the pipeline, silent wrong output is the main risk of codifying agent procedures into scripts.

Task quality is fixed by construction in the simulation: 'When a program fails, the model uses the same agent outcome as ReAct for that arrival. This rule ensures that task success in the model cannot be lower than ReAct's' (App. C.3). The online evaluation therefore cannot reveal any quality cost of compiling. Drift is also reported to the policy by the environment, i.e. oracle drift detection.

Brittleness: interruptions (notification, low battery, permission dialog, update prompt) make 83–100% of verified programs fail (A.7). GLM Contacts passed 30/30 deployment tasks but failed 5/5 on a rebuilt emulator (A.6).

Live evidence is thin. The only live comparison (App. D) is 12 paired Calendar tasks with a fixed program, and its 95% envelope for the serving-cost difference, [-33.0, 4.6] milli-USD, includes zero (D.3). The online compilation algorithm itself is never run live.

The '2–16 uses' payback excludes failed attempts, trace collection and replacement after drift (Table 1 caption). The trace-inclusive range is 4.4–18.7, and it rests on a single cost record per cell (A.8).
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats and with every score. The budget guarantee is real but only relative to a modeled reference under assumed charge bounds, so I graded it moderate rather than strong. The compile-to-code (P33) supports stance ignores survivorship and the fact that eager compilation costs more than never compiling. The paper's own App. A.7 silent-failure rate is the most relevant warning for a team considering 'promote repeated agent work to scripts'.
